# A Comprehensive Research Report on Dorfromantik

## Origins and Development

*Dorfromantik* represents a unique case study in modern game development, encompassing two distinct but deeply interconnected products: a video game and a board game adaptation [)]. The narrative of its creation is not a simple tale of licensing but a story of serendipity, thematic synergy, and deliberate adaptation that bridges the worlds of digital and tabletop gaming , . The origins of the entire *Dorfromantik* universe lie with the Berlin-based indie game studio Toukana Interactive, founded in 2020 by four individuals who met while studying Game Design at HTW Berlin (the University of Applied Sciences) , . The founding team consisted of Timo Falcke, Sandro Heuberger, Luca Langenberg, and Zwi Zausch . Their collaborative journey began as a master's thesis project, where they engaged in a rapid prototyping phase characterized by building a new game concept every two or three days over approximately three weeks . During this intense ideation period, they developed around ten distinct concepts before one emerged with exceptional promise . This prototype would become the foundation for the original *Dorfromantik* video game.

The name 'Dorfromantik' itself was adopted during this initial development phase and carries significant thematic weight; it is a German word meaning "the nostalgic feeling you get when you long to be in the countryside," or more broadly, "village romanticization" , . This placeholder name was retained because it resonated strongly with the developers' artistic intent for the game: to evoke calmness, creativity, and a sense of peaceful coexistence between civilization and nature , . The core mechanics of this standout prototype were implemented remarkably quickly, taking only two days to establish a functional loop centered on hexagonal tile-laying with side-matching, mission-based scoring, and scalable landscape expansion . This clear vision and solid mechanical foundation distinguished it from their other prototypes . The game originated as a Ludum Dare game jam entry in late April 2020, built under the theme "Keep it Alive," which focused on balancing civilization and nature through tile placement . It evolved into a more expansive landscape-building mechanic with quests tied to counting connected elements, such as fulfilling character-driven demands like "the deer wants to live in a forest with at least X trees" . The video game entered Early Access on Steam and GOG in March 2021 and was released as a full version on April 28, 2022, for PC platforms [), , ]. The game's aesthetic draws inspiration from Romantic-era art, Impressionism, and classic board games, reinforcing its bucolic and idyllic feel .

While Toukana was developing their video game, another set of creators was pursuing a parallel path that would ultimately lead to the board game adaptation. Lukas Zach and Michael Palm are the credited designers of *Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel* , . For over two decades, Zach and Palm had been collaborating on board game designs, maintaining a remote working relationship despite not living near each other . At the time they discovered the video game, they were already working on their own long-in-developed hexagonal tile-placement prototype, which was set in a South Seas theme . They first encountered the video game when it was nominated for the Deutsche Computerspielepreis alongside another title named *Iron Harvest* . Upon seeing it, Zach recognized its "board-game-ish" feel and noted its thematic alignment with their own work-in-progress . This sparked the idea of an adaptation. They initiated contact with Pegasus Spiele, the publisher of their previous games, and also reached out to Toukana Interactive, proposing a collaboration . Interestingly, Toukana had also considered a board game adaptation themselves, with developer Sandro Heuberger acknowledging the possibility in a 2021 interview, stating, "We have considered it. Who knows. Maybe there will be something along those lines (laughs)" . This shared interest created a fertile ground for partnership. The board game was explicitly based on and named after the 2022 video game, marking a rare instance where a physical game was conceived and developed specifically because its creators saw a strong potential for translation from a successful digital source [), ].

The development process culminated in a first in-person collaboration between the Zach/Palm and Toukana teams at Essen SPIEL in 2022, where the board game was publicly playable for the first time [), ]. The board game was published by Pegasus Spiele, a well-known German publisher [), ]. The original German-language release occurred in November 2022, followed by the English-language release in October 2023 [)]. The game was illustrated by Paul Riebe, who worked on both the video game and board game versions, ensuring a high degree of visual consistency across the two formats , . This close collaboration extended to the game's design philosophy, which blended Zach and Palm's expertise in board game design with the established themes and mechanics of the original digital title . The result was a product that successfully translated the "cozy vibes" and tranquil experience of the video game into a tangible, social tabletop format . The game's success has been notable enough for Zach to confirm ongoing plans for further expansion within the *Dorfromantik* universe, including the upcoming *Dorfromantik: Das Duell*, indicating a long-term commitment to the intellectual property . The entire development arc, from the university project in Berlin to the international award ceremony, highlights a remarkable convergence of creative minds and mediums, resulting in a product that holds a unique place in contemporary game history .

## Core Gameplay Mechanics

The core gameplay of *Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel* is a cooperative tile-laying experience designed to be accessible yet strategically engaging , . It is intended for one to six players, with a recommended age of eight and over, and typically lasts between 30 and 60 minutes per session [), ]. The fundamental premise of the game is to collaboratively construct a scenic European countryside by placing hexagonal landscape tiles adjacent to one another , . Players never lose; the game concludes when the draw pile of landscape tiles is exhausted, and all participants effectively "win" by having successfully built a cohesive and aesthetically pleasing map . Meaningful tension and strategic depth arise not from competition or failure, but from self-imposed goals, such as maximizing the final score, completing challenging tasks, and enclosing large areas of terrain with flag tiles . The game's design encourages a calm, almost meditative state of play, often described as "solving a jigsaw puzzle together" to build an ever-growing village of the players' collective creation . Each turn follows a simple and consistent core loop: players draw one tile from a stack and then place it adjacent to the existing layout on the table, connecting edge-to-edge with at least one other tile , .

The game's components are carefully designed to facilitate this creative process. The playing area begins empty and grows organically as players add tiles. There are five distinct types of landscape tiles: forests, grain fields, villages, rivers, and train tracks , . These are hexagonal in shape, allowing for multiple connection points. A key rule governing placement is that rivers must connect only to other rivers, and train tracks must connect only to other train tracks; other terrain types, such as forests, fields, and villages, may abut freely against any other terrain type , . This creates natural pathways for water and transport networks across the evolving landscape. To guide and challenge the players, the game utilizes two main types of special tiles: Task tiles (also referred to as Quest tiles) and Flag tiles , . At any given time, three Task tiles are kept face-up and in play on the table . Each of these five-task types requires players to create a specific, enclosed region of matching terrain type with a precise number of connected tiles , . For example, a task might require players to build a forest that is exactly five tiles big, or a field that contains at least seven tiles . When a player completes a task by making the required number of connections, they claim the corresponding Task Marker, which remains face-down until the end of the game to prevent premature point manipulation . Completing a task scores one point for each tile that fulfilled the objective, providing a direct incentive to complete objectives efficiently .

Beyond the primary task of completing objectives, the game offers several additional layers of scoring to encourage diverse strategies and reward different aspects of the constructed landscape. One such mechanism involves Flag tiles. These special tiles are placed by players to mark off fully enclosed, contiguous regions of a single terrain type—forests, fields, or villages—that have no open edges connecting to the outside world , . At the end of the game, players score one point for every tile within each completed flagged region . This introduces a powerful strategic choice: players must decide whether to prioritize filling tasks or to invest moves in building large, closed-off territories for future flag-scoring opportunities. Another layer of scoring rewards the most extensive linear features on the map. The player who has built the longest continuous river and the longest continuous train track each earns points equal to the number of tiles in that feature , . This encourages players to think about the overall structure and connectivity of their growing landscape, rather than focusing solely on isolated tasks. Finally, the game incorporates the concept of "perfect tiles," represented by wooden Hearts . When a player places a tile in such a way that it matches its surrounding terrain on all six of its edges, they receive a Heart token. While Hearts do not contribute directly to the final score, they serve as a form of positive reinforcement and are used to fulfill special conditions, adding a subtle but satisfying element of discovery and reward to the gameplay loop , .

The board game's designers made conscious decisions to adapt the mechanics from the original video game to suit the constraints and strengths of the tabletop medium. One of the most significant changes was the simplification of the digital game's complex scoring system . The video game featured granular calculations, such as awarding points for each individual tree or for the number of edges matched, which would be impractical to manage physically , . Instead, the board game replaced these with a simpler, tile-count-based approach for task completion, making it easier for players to tally points without constant calculation . However, the board game enhances strategic depth in other ways. For instance, it introduces new components and even modifies rules as players progress through the campaign system, whereas the video game's unlocks were primarily cosmetic . The board game also retains key digital concepts like "perfect tiles" and buildings that can double task values in designated zones, but adapts them for physical implementation . This thoughtful adaptation demonstrates a deep understanding of both mediums, preserving the spirit and core appeal of the original while optimizing the experience for a group of people sitting around a table. The result is a game that is easy to learn but difficult to master, offering a rich and rewarding experience for a wide audience, from casual players to experienced gamers .

## The Campaign Progression System

Perhaps the most innovative and defining feature of *Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel* is its resettable campaign progression system, which transforms the game from a static collection of components into a dynamic, evolving experience , . This system mirrors the unlockable content and campaign structure found in the original video game, representing a successful transposition of a digital mechanic into a physical format , . The core of this system is a modular storage insert included in the base game box, which contains five sealed plastic boxes , . These boxes are filled with additional components that expand the game's strategic possibilities, including 32 extra landscape tiles, 31 cards, 8 markers, 5 wooden Hearts, and 1 plastic stand , . The campaign is managed using a dedicated Campaign Sheet Pad, which consists of twenty one-sided sheets , . After each game session, players log their final score (rounded down to the nearest ten) on this pad . This score determines how far along a branching campaign trail they advance, allowing them to cross off circles on the sheet to unlock new content , . As players accumulate points over successive games, they progressively gain access to the contents of the sealed boxes, introducing new tiles, new tasks, new rules, and new objectives into the game pool , .

This progression system is engineered to increase the complexity and replayability of the game organically. Higher scores lead to faster unlocking of new content, creating a virtuous cycle where success in the game provides more tools and challenges for future sessions , . Conversely, lower scores slow down the progression, but crucially, there are no penalties for failing to unlock a box; players simply continue trying in subsequent games . This ensures that the campaign remains accessible and non-frustrating for players of all skill levels. The system is explicitly resettable, a key distinction from traditional legacy games that often involve irreversible changes like permanently altering rulebooks or destroying components . At the end of a campaign run, all unlocked components must be meticulously returned to their respective sealed boxes, and the Campaign Sheet Pad is reset, restoring the game to its original base state , . This resettable nature makes the campaign system highly appealing to a broad audience, as it allows players to experience the expanded content without committing to permanent alterations of the game, thereby lowering the barrier to entry for those wary of legacy-style games . The campaign system is not merely a collection of new parts; it fundamentally alters the strategic landscape. Unlocking new tiles and achievement cards grants players permanent upgrades, such as special locomotives and ships, which are cosmetic homages to the digital game but also introduce new scoring mechanisms and placement restrictions in the board game context . Unlike the digital version where unlocks are purely cosmetic, the board game's unlocks actively change how the game is played, increasing its strategic depth across replay sessions . This careful balance of expanding options without breaking the game's foundational simplicity is a testament to the thoughtful design of Zach and Palm. The system provides a structured goal for repeated play, encouraging players to experiment with new combinations of tiles and strategies, and fostering a sense of long-term engagement and discovery . The inclusion of this sophisticated, resettable campaign system was a major factor in the game's critical acclaim and its historic win at the Spiel des Jahres award , .

## Critical Reception and Industry Significance

The critical reception of *Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel* has been overwhelmingly positive, culminating in one of the most prestigious awards in the tabletop gaming industry. Its most significant accolade came on July 16, 2023, when it was announced as the winner of the Spiel des Jahres (Game of the Year) award for 2023 , . The Spiel des Jahres award is a highly respected annual prize in Germany, judged by a panel of journalists and prominent game reviewers, aimed at recognizing excellence in board game design and broad accessibility . The announcement took place at a ceremony in Berlin, where the game was selected from a shortlist of nominees that included titles like *Fun Facts* and *Next Station London* , . Public voting conducted in conjunction with the award showed an overwhelming preference for *Dorfromantik*, with 82% of the 263 votes cast favoring it as the ultimate winner . The jury's official rationale for selecting the game highlighted several groundbreaking aspects of its design. They praised its successful adaptation of the digital video game's campaign structure into a compelling physical format and emphasized its strong appeal to non-gamers, aligning perfectly with the Spiel des Jahres award's mission to broaden participation in tabletop gaming .

The significance of *Dorfromantik*'s victory extends beyond its immediate critical acclaim; it marked several historical firsts for the award. Multiple sources confirmed that *Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel* became the very first winner in the history of the Spiel des Jahres to be an adaptation of a video game . Furthermore, it was the first-ever winner to incorporate legacy-style components that unlock new elements and challenges over time, albeit in a resettable manner , . These two factors alone position the game as a pivotal moment in the evolution of board games, demonstrating the viability and creativity of adapting digital-native experiences for the tabletop and innovating upon the legacy genre. The win underscored a growing trend of crossover influence between digital and physical games, a trend that the game itself exemplifies so perfectly. Beyond the Spiel des Jahres, the game has maintained a strong presence in the gaming community. On BoardGameGeek, a leading platform for board game information, it holds a rating of 7.6/10 and ranked #75 in the site's Top 100 Solo Board Games list for 2024, climbing from #136 in the previous year's ranking, a testament to its enduring appeal , .

The critical reception of the original *Dorfromantik* video game, which served as the source material, was also favorable. Polygon magazine included it in its Top 50 Games of 2022 list, ranking it at #41 . The publication described the game as a "zenlike, cooperative-feeling tile-laying game" that emphasizes peaceful, emergent settlement over rigid planning, capturing the "cozy vibes" that define the franchise . This positive reception of the digital original helped build the foundation of goodwill and anticipation that undoubtedly contributed to the success of the board game adaptation. Reviewers of the board game itself consistently highlight its elegant design and relaxing atmosphere. Shut Up & Sit Down, a popular game review channel, captured the essence of the game by describing it as "capturing the feeling of sitting down and solving a jigsaw puzzle together" . Another reviewer purchasing the game shortly after its release praised its ease of entry, giving it a perfect five-star rating for "Ease of entry" and expressing a firm intention to play it again, noting it had become his and his wife's go-to game for free time . The game's cooperative nature, lack of real stakes, and focus on collective creativity are frequently cited as its greatest strengths, making it an ideal gateway game for families and newcomers to the hobby , . The combination of top-tier award recognition, sustained community engagement, and widespread critical praise has firmly established *Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel* as a landmark title in modern board game design.

## Ecosystem and Expansions

Since its initial release, the *Dorfromantik* franchise has grown beyond its original board game, developing a small but meaningful ecosystem of expansions and spin-offs that demonstrate its commercial viability and lasting appeal. The most significant addition to the franchise is *Dorfromantik: The Duel*, a standalone competitive two-player (or two-team) game released on April 9, 2024 . Designed by the same duo, Lukas Zach and Michael Palm, *The Duel* fundamentally reimagines the core gameplay loop by transforming the cooperative landscape-building experience into a head-to-head contest , . In this version, players still lay hexagonal tiles to build their respective worlds, but now compete to complete tasks and score points to create the most beautiful world, introducing a new layer of tactical interaction and conflict . The game features a substantial component count, including 157 landscape tiles and 61 task markers, alongside new card types, camera markers for tracking achievements, and special photographer-themed tiles . *The Duel* serves as a testament to the robustness of the underlying mechanics, proving that they can be adapted to support different play styles, from serene cooperation to tense competition.

In addition to the major expansion, Pegasus Spiele has also released officially licensed mini-expansions that add localized flavor and variety to the base game. One such product is the *Wetterau Mini-Erweiterung*, released on June 21, 2024 . This expansion package contains three new special tiles featuring regional motifs from the Hessian Wetterau, including Adolfsturm, Pegasus, and Winterstein with its iconic Steinkopf-Fernsehturm tower . Each of these special tiles comes with unique rules, integrating them seamlessly into the existing gameplay framework . The existence of such officially supported, regionally themed expansions indicates a publisher committed to supporting the game's long-term health and catering to fans who enjoy collecting and customizing their gaming experience. These smaller additions provide fresh strategic elements and aesthetic variations without requiring a complete overhaul of the game, keeping the experience feeling new and exciting for returning players.

The influence of *Dorfromantik* extends beyond its own product line, cementing its role as a cultural touchstone within the game design community. The game has been explicitly cited as a key inspiration by other indie game developers, highlighting its importance in shaping the current landscape of digital games influenced by tabletop principles . Jean-Baptiste Oger, game director of Drop Duchy and founder of Sleepy Mill, identified *Dorfromantik* as a significant influence during his development process, placing it alongside classics like *Carcassonne* and *Cartographers* . He praised the game for its role in shaping his own tile-placement mechanics and the "tactile tension" he sought to achieve in his own titles, reinforcing *Dorfromantik*'s status as a bridge between digital and physical game design . This external validation underscores the game's impact, showing that its success was not just a commercial phenomenon but also a design milestone that has informed and inspired other creators in the industry. This combination of internal expansion through new game modes and external influence on the broader design community speaks to the strength and versatility of the original concept, suggesting that the *Dorfromantik* universe is poised for continued growth and relevance.

## Comparative Analysis and Design Philosophy

The design philosophy behind *Dorfromantik* is rooted in a deliberate effort to translate the emotional and aesthetic qualities of a digital experience into a tangible, social tabletop format. The game’s core identity is defined by its emphasis on "cozy vibes," calmness, and player-driven creativity , . This contrasts sharply with many traditional board games that rely on high-stakes competition, resource management, or complex strategic negotiations. Instead, *Dorfromantik* prioritizes the act of collaborative creation, offering players a safe space where failure is not a punitive event but an integral part of the emergent storytelling . The designers, Lukas Zach and Michael Palm, achieved this by focusing on a simple, intuitive core loop—draw and place a tile—and layering it with optional goals and scoring systems that cater to different play styles , . This approach lowers the barrier to entry significantly, making the game accessible to a wide audience, including families and individuals who may be new to board gaming . The game's success lies in its ability to foster a sense of shared accomplishment and quiet satisfaction, a feeling often described as akin to building something beautiful together with friends .

A central aspect of the game's design is its innovative approach to progression and replayability, embodied by its resettable campaign system. This mechanic stands in contrast to many legacy games that impose irreversible changes, which can be intimidating to new players and limit the game's accessibility . By making the campaign entirely resettable, Zach and Palm created a system that encourages experimentation and long-term engagement without the fear of "breaking" the game . Players can unlock new components, test new strategies, and experience the evolving game without any permanent consequences, making it an ideal vehicle for discovering the full depth of the game's mechanics. This design choice reflects a broader philosophy of inclusivity and player empowerment, giving players control over their pace of exploration and learning. The system is not a forced march toward a predetermined conclusion but a flexible framework for discovery, where players can choose to push for higher scores to unlock faster or simply enjoy the process at their own rhythm .

When compared to other popular tile-laying games, *Dorfromantik* distinguishes itself through its unique blend of cooperative play and structured progression. While games like *Carcassonne* also involve placing tiles to create a shared map, *Dorfromantik*'s focus on enclosed areas for scoring (flags) and linear features (rivers, tracks) provides a different set of strategic incentives . The introduction of the task system adds a layer of micro-objective fulfillment that guides the flow of the game, preventing the map from becoming a haphazard collection of shapes. The game's most profound comparison, however, is with its own digital predecessor. The board game successfully preserves the core DNA of the video game—the tranquil, contemplative pace and the joy of watching a landscape emerge from simple, repeated actions—but enhances it with the tactile feedback and social interaction inherent to physical games . The adaptation involved smart concessions, such as simplifying the scoring system, while simultaneously enriching the experience through the campaign system, which introduces novel strategic elements not present in the original digital version . In summary, the design philosophy of *Dorfromantik* is one of thoughtful synthesis. It takes the best elements of digital game design—its focus on aesthetics, emotional resonance, and progressive revelation—and grafts them onto the social fabric of a classic board game mechanic. This fusion has resulted in a product that feels both familiar and refreshingly new, earning it a special place in the hearts of players and the annals of board game history.

Completing a task in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel scores one point for each tile that fulfilled the objective.
The scoring for completing a task provides a direct incentive to complete objectives efficiently.

Beyond the primary task of completing objectives, Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel offers several additional layers of scoring to encourage diverse strategies and reward different aspects of the constructed landscape.
One additional scoring mechanism in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel involves Flag tiles.

Flag tiles in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel are placed by players to mark off fully enclosed, contiguous regions of a single terrain type—forests, fields, or villages—that have no open edges connecting to the outside world.
At the end of Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel, players score one point for every tile within each completed flagged region.

The Flag tile mechanism introduces a powerful strategic choice in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel: players must decide whether to prioritize filling tasks or to invest moves in building large, closed-off territories for future flag-scoring opportunities.
Another layer of scoring in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel rewards the most extensive linear features on the map.
The player who has built the longest continuous river and the longest continuous train track in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel each earns points equal to the number of tiles in that feature.
This scoring mechanism encourages players to think about the overall structure and connectivity of their growing landscape, rather than focusing solely on isolated tasks.
Finally, Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel incorporates the concept of "perfect tiles," represented by wooden Hearts.
When a player places a tile in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel in such a way that it matches its surrounding terrain on all six of its edges, they receive a Heart token.
While Hearts do not contribute directly to the final score in Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel, they serve as a form of positive reinforcement and are used to fulfill special conditions.
Hearts add a subtle but satisfying element of discovery and reward to the gameplay loop of Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel.
The Dorfromantik board game's designers made conscious decisions to adapt the mechanics from the original video game to suit the constraints and strengths of the tabletop medium.
One of the most significant changes in the Dorfromantik board game adaptation was the simplification of the digital game's complex scoring system.
The Dorfromantik video game featured granular calculations, such as awarding points for each individual tree or for the number of edges matched, which would be impractical to manage physically.

Instead, the Dorfromantik board game replaced granular calculations with a simpler, tile-count-based approach for task completion, making it easier for players to tally points without constant calculation.
However, the Dorfromantik board game enhances strategic depth in other ways.
For instance, the Dorfromantik board game introduces new components and even modifies rules as players progress through the campaign system, whereas the video game's unlocks were primarily cosmetic.
The Dorfromantik board game also retains key digital concepts like "perfect tiles" and buildings that can double task values in designated zones, but adapts them for physical implementation.

This thoughtful adaptation demonstrates a deep understanding of both mediums, preserving the spirit and core appeal of the original while optimizing the experience for a group of people sitting around a table.
The result is a game that is easy to learn but difficult to master, offering a rich and rewarding experience for a wide audience, from casual players to experienced gamers.

Perhaps the most innovative and defining feature of Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel is its resettable campaign progression system, which transforms the game from a static collection of components into a dynamic, evolving experience.
This system mirrors the unlockable content and campaign structure found in the original video game, representing a successful transposition of a digital mechanic into a physical format.
The core of this system is a modular storage insert included in the base game box, which contains five sealed plastic boxes.
These boxes are filled with additional components that expand the game's strategic possibilities, including 32 extra landscape tiles, 31 cards, 8 markers, 5 wooden Hearts, and 1 plastic stand.
The campaign is managed using a dedicated Campaign Sheet Pad, which consists of twenty one-sided sheets.
After each game session, players log their final score (rounded down to the nearest ten) on this pad.
This score determines how far along a branching campaign trail they advance, allowing them to cross off circles on the sheet to unlock new content.

As players accumulate points over successive games, they progressively gain access to the contents of the sealed boxes, introducing new tiles, new tasks, new rules, and new objectives into the game pool.
This progression system is engineered to increase the complexity and replayability of the game organically.
Higher scores lead to faster unlocking of new content, creating a virtuous cycle where success in the game provides more tools and challenges for future sessions.
Conversely, lower scores slow down the progression, but crucially, there are no penalties for failing to unlock a box; players simply continue trying in subsequent games.
This ensures that the campaign remains accessible and non-frustrating for players of all skill levels.
The system is explicitly resettable, a key distinction from traditional legacy games that often involve irreversible changes like permanently altering rulebooks or destroying components.

At the end of a campaign run, all unlocked components must be meticulously returned to their respective sealed boxes, and the Campaign Sheet Pad is reset, restoring the game to its original base state.

This resettable nature makes the campaign system highly appealing to a broad audience, as it allows players to experience the expanded content without committing to permanent alterations of the game, thereby lowering the barrier to entry for those wary of legacy-style games.
The campaign system is not merely a collection of new parts; it fundamentally alters the strategic landscape.

Unlocking new tiles and achievement cards grants players permanent upgrades, such as special locomotives and ships, which are cosmetic homages to the digital game but also introduce new scoring mechanisms and placement restrictions in the board game context.
Unlike the digital version where unlocks are purely cosmetic, the board game's unlocks actively change how the game is played, increasing its strategic depth across replay sessions.
This careful balance of expanding options without breaking the game's foundational simplicity is a testament to the thoughtful design of Zach and Palm.
The system provides a structured goal for repeated play, encouraging players to experiment with new combinations of tiles and strategies, and fostering a sense of long-term engagement and discovery.
The inclusion of this sophisticated, resettable campaign system was a major factor in the game's critical acclaim and its historic win at the Spiel des Jahres award.
The Dorfromantik base game includes 48 hexagonal tiles depicting forests, grain, villages, streams, and tracks.
The Dorfromantik base game includes 25 Task tiles (five of each terrain type).
The Dorfromantik base game includes 1 plastic stand.
The Dorfromantik base game includes 25 Task Markers.
The Dorfromantik base game includes 2 storage boards.
The Dorfromantik base game includes 1 Score Pad (50 sheets, two-sided).
The Dorfromantik base game includes 1 Campaign Sheet Pad (20 one-sided sheets).
The Dorfromantik base game includes 1 Rulebook.
The Dorfromantik base game includes a modular insert with labeled compartments.
The sealed boxes in Dorfromantik include 32 additional landscape tiles.
The sealed boxes in Dorfromantik include 31 cards.
The sealed boxes in Dorfromantik include 36 Camera markers.
The sealed boxes in Dorfromantik include 1 Photographer tile.
The sealed boxes in Dorfromantik include 5 wooden Hearts.
The critical reception of Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel has been overwhelmingly positive, culminating in one of the most prestigious awards in the tabletop gaming industry.
Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel's most significant accolade came on July 16, 2023, when it was announced as the winner of the Spiel des Jahres (Game of the Year) award for 2023.

The Spiel des Jahres award is a highly respected annual prize in Germany, judged by a panel of journalists and prominent game reviewers, aimed at recognizing excellence in board game design and broad accessibility.

The announcement of the Spiel des Jahres award took place at a ceremony in Berlin, where Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel was selected from a shortlist of nominees that included titles like Fun Facts and Next Station London.
Public voting conducted in conjunction with the Spiel des Jahres award showed an overwhelming preference for Dorfromantik, with 82% of the 263 votes cast favoring it as the ultimate winner.
The jury's official rationale for selecting Dorfromantik highlighted several groundbreaking aspects of its design.
The jury praised Dorfromantik's successful adaptation of the digital video game's campaign structure into a compelling physical format.
The jury emphasized Dorfromantik's strong appeal to non-gamers, aligning perfectly with the Spiel des Jahres award's mission to broaden participation in tabletop gaming.
The significance of Dorfromantik's victory extends beyond its immediate critical acclaim; it marked several historical firsts for the award.
Multiple sources confirmed that Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel became the very first winner in the history of the Spiel des Jahres to be an adaptation of a video game.
Furthermore, Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel was the first-ever winner to incorporate legacy-style components that unlock new elements and challenges over time, albeit in a resettable manner.

These two factors alone position the game as a pivotal moment in the evolution of board games, demonstrating the viability and creativity of adapting digital-native experiences for the tabletop and innovating upon the legacy genre.
The win underscored a growing trend of crossover influence between digital and physical games, a trend that the game itself exemplifies so perfectly.
Beyond the Spiel des Jahres, the game has maintained a strong presence in the gaming community.
On BoardGameGeek, a leading platform for board game information, Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel holds a rating of 7.6/10.
Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel ranked #75 in BoardGameGeek's Top 100 Solo Board Games list for 2024, climbing from #136 in the previous year's ranking, a testament to its enduring appeal.
The critical reception of the original Dorfromantik video game, which served as the source material, was also favorable.
Polygon magazine included the Dorfromantik video game in its Top 50 Games of 2022 list, ranking it at #41.

Polygon described the Dorfromantik video game as a "zenlike, cooperative-feeling tile-laying game" that emphasizes peaceful, emergent settlement over rigid planning, capturing the "cozy vibes" that define the franchise.
This positive reception of the digital original helped build the foundation of goodwill and anticipation that undoubtedly contributed to the success of the board game adaptation.
Reviewers of the board game itself consistently highlight its elegant design and relaxing atmosphere.
Shut Up & Sit Down, a popular game review channel, captured the essence of the game by describing it as "capturing the feeling of sitting down and solving a jigsaw puzzle together."

Another reviewer purchasing the game shortly after its release praised its ease of entry, giving it a perfect five-star rating for "Ease of entry" and expressing a firm intention to play it again, noting it had become his and his wife's go-to game for free time.

The game's cooperative nature, lack of real stakes, and focus on collective creativity are frequently cited as its greatest strengths, making it an ideal gateway game for families and newcomers to the hobby.

The combination of top-tier award recognition, sustained community engagement, and widespread critical praise has firmly established Dorfromantik: Das Brettspiel as a landmark title in modern board game design.

Since its initial release, the Dorfromantik franchise has grown beyond its original board game, developing a small but meaningful ecosystem of expansions and spin-offs that demonstrate its commercial viability and lasting appeal.
The most significant addition to the franchise is Dorfromantik: The Duel, a standalone competitive two-player (or two-team) game released on April 9, 2024.
Dorfromantik: The Duel is designed by the same duo, Lukas Zach and Michael Palm.
Dorfromantik: The Duel fundamentally reimagines the core gameplay loop by transforming the cooperative landscape-building experience into a head-to-head contest.

In Dorfromantik: The Duel, players still lay hexagonal tiles to build their respective worlds, but now compete to complete tasks and score points to create the most beautiful world, introducing a new layer of tactical interaction and conflict.

Dorfromantik: The Duel features a substantial component count, including 157 landscape tiles and 61 task markers, alongside new card types, camera markers for tracking achievements, and special photographer-themed tiles.

Dorfromantik: The Duel serves as a testament to the robustness of the underlying mechanics, proving that they can be adapted to support different play styles, from serene cooperation to tense competition.
In addition to the major expansion, Pegasus Spiele has also released officially licensed mini-expansions that add localized flavor and variety to the base game.
One such product is the Wetterau Mini-Erweiterung, released on June 21, 2024.

This expansion package contains three new special tiles featuring regional motifs from the Hessian Wetterau, including Adolfsturm, Pegasus, and Winterstein with its iconic Steinkopf-Fernsehturm tower.
Each of these special tiles comes with unique rules, integrating them seamlessly into the existing gameplay framework.

The existence of such officially supported, regionally themed expansions indicates a publisher committed to supporting the game's long-term health and catering to fans who enjoy collecting and customizing their gaming experience.

These smaller additions provide fresh strategic elements and aesthetic variations without requiring a complete overhaul of the game, keeping the experience feeling new and exciting for returning players.
The influence of Dorfromantik extends beyond its own product line, cementing its role as a cultural touchstone within the game design community.

The game has been explicitly cited as a key inspiration by other indie game developers, highlighting its importance in shaping the current landscape of digital games influenced by tabletop principles.

Jean-Baptiste Oger, game director of Drop Duchy and founder of Sleepy Mill, identified Dorfromantik as a significant influence during his development process, placing it alongside classics like Carcassonne and Cartographers.

Jean-Baptiste Oger praised Dorfromantik for its role in shaping his own tile-placement mechanics and the "tactile tension" he sought to achieve in his own titles, reinforcing Dorfromantik's status as a bridge between digital and physical game design.

This external validation underscores the game's impact, showing that its success was not just a commercial phenomenon but also a design milestone that has informed and inspired other creators in the industry.

This combination of internal expansion through new game modes and external influence on the broader design community speaks to the strength and versatility of the original concept, suggesting that the Dorfromantik universe is poised for continued growth and relevance.
The design philosophy behind Dorfromantik is rooted in a deliberate effort to translate the emotional and aesthetic qualities of a digital experience into a tangible, social tabletop format.
The game’s core identity is defined by its emphasis on "cozy vibes," calmness, and player-driven creativity.
This contrasts sharply with many traditional board games that rely on high-stakes competition, resource management, or complex strategic negotiations.
Instead, Dorfromantik prioritizes the act of collaborative creation, offering players a safe space where failure is not a punitive event but an integral part of the emergent storytelling.

The designers, Lukas Zach and Michael Palm, achieved this by focusing on a simple, intuitive core loop—draw and place a tile—and layering it with optional goals and scoring systems that cater to different play styles.
This approach lowers the barrier to entry significantly, making the game accessible to a wide audience, including families and individuals who may be new to board gaming.
The game's success lies in its ability to foster a sense of shared accomplishment and quiet satisfaction, a feeling often described as akin to building something beautiful together with friends.
A central aspect of the game's design is its innovative approach to progression and replayability, embodied by its resettable campaign system.
This mechanic stands in contrast to many legacy games that impose irreversible changes, which can be intimidating to new players and limit the game's accessibility.
By making the campaign entirely resettable, Zach and Palm created a system that encourages experimentation and long-term engagement without the fear of "breaking" the game.

Players can unlock new components, test new strategies, and experience the evolving game without any permanent consequences, making it an ideal vehicle for discovering the full depth of the game's mechanics.
This design choice reflects a broader philosophy of inclusivity and player empowerment, giving players control over their pace of exploration and learning.

The system is not a forced march toward a predetermined conclusion but a flexible framework for discovery, where players can choose to push for higher scores to unlock faster or simply enjoy the process at their own rhythm.
When compared to other popular tile-laying games, Dorfromantik distinguishes itself through its unique blend of cooperative play and structured progression.

While games like Carcassonne also involve placing tiles to create a shared map, Dorfromantik's focus on enclosed areas for scoring (flags) and linear features (rivers, tracks) provides a different set of strategic incentives.
The introduction of the task system adds a layer of micro-objective fulfillment that guides the flow of the game, preventing the map from becoming a haphazard collection of shapes.
The game's most profound comparison, however, is with its own digital predecessor.

The board game successfully preserves the core DNA of the video game—the tranquil, contemplative pace and the joy of watching a landscape emerge from simple, repeated actions—but enhances it with the tactile feedback and social interaction inherent to physical games.

The adaptation involved smart concessions, such as simplifying the scoring system, while simultaneously enriching the experience through the campaign system, which introduces novel strategic elements not present in the original digital version.
In summary, the design philosophy of Dorfromantik is one of thoughtful synthesis.
It takes the best elements of digital game design—its focus on aesthetics, emotional resonance, and progressive revelation—and grafts them onto the social fabric of a classic board game mechanic.
This fusion has resulted in a product that feels both familiar and refreshingly new, earning it a special place in the hearts of players and the annals of board game history.

Sparking joy through tile placement in idyllic village builder _Dorfromantik_
=============================================================================

"One of our core philosophies when making games is that the interaction the player does the most has to feel as satisfying as possible."

[![Image 11: Picture of Joel Couture](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/bltef4298d364a9bfa1/6508832dca23d12f34840106/Joel_Couture.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/author/joel-couture)

[Joel Couture](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/author/joel-couture), ContributorJuly 19, 2021

6 Min Read

![Image 12: Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/bltba62518415cda0e2/652fe6ddbc479f8697ef691f/default-cubic.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&format=jpg&disable=upscale)

[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/sparking-joy-through-tile-placement-in-idyllic-village-builder-i-dorfromantik-i-)[](http://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/sparking-joy-through-tile-placement-in-idyllic-village-builder-i-dorfromantik-i-)[](http://www.twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/sparking-joy-through-tile-placement-in-idyllic-village-builder-i-dorfromantik-i-)[](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/sparking-joy-through-tile-placement-in-idyllic-village-builder-i-dorfromantik-i-&title=Sparking%20joy%20through%20tile%20placement%20in%20idyllic%20village%20builder%20Dorfromantik)[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=Sparking%20joy%20through%20tile%20placement%20in%20idyllic%20village%20builder%20_Dorfromantik_%20-%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.gamedeveloper.com%2Fbusiness%2Fsparking-joy-through-tile-placement-in-idyllic-village-builder-i-dorfromantik-i-)[](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#)

This interview is part of our Road to the IGF series.

[Dorfromantik](https://store.steampowered.com/app/1455840/Dorfromantik/) creates peaceful villages through placing tiles, steadily creating a living landscape based around where you place forests, rivers, houses, train  tracks, and more.

Gamasutra sat down with Timo Falcke of Toukana Interactive, developers of the Best Student Game-nominated title, to learn about how they worked to create a feeling of peacefulness within the game, the board game inspirations that shaped the game, and creating appeal in even the smallest interaction with the gameplay.

Who are you, and what was your role in developing Dorfromantik?
===============================================================

My name is Timo Falcke. I'm one of the four members of Toukana Interactive, the studio behind Dorfromantik. My primary role on our team is as the programmer, but I'm also majorly involved in Game Design and in managing our accounting on the side.

The other team members are Luca Langenberg, Sandro Heuberger, and Zwi Zausch, all of them with a primary and several secondary roles.

Together with Luca, Sandro, and Zwi, I studied for my Bachelor's degree in Game Design at HTW Berlin. We developed several games as semester projects, and Sandro and I completed one and released it commercially on Steam: the VR game ViSP - Virtual Space Port. Besides that, I took part in many Game Jams and developed smaller games for those, some alone, some in various team constellations. I also enjoy developing board games as a hobby, though I haven't pursued releasing any one of them so far.

Since 2020, all four of us are studying in the Games Master's program at HTW Berlin and will write our Master's thesis about the process of making Dorfromantik.

![Image 13](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/blte1255f46d7ff17c9/650e781019ec0e643d9fbb9c/Dorfromantik_202.jpg/?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

How did you come up with the concept for Dorfromantik? 
=======================================================

In April 2020 we were in our first semester of our Master's program and also in the ideation phase for the first game we would develop as Toukana Interactive. During that time, we developed more than 10 different prototypes, and Dorfromantik was one of them.

The first Dorfromantik prototype originated in the Ludum Dare game jam at the end of April, with the theme "Keep it Alive". After brainstorming different approaches for this topic, we liked the idea of keeping a civilization alive by balancing it out with its surrounding nature. Since we wanted to find a simple, yet very scalable core mechanic, we had the idea of forming a simplified landscape by placing tiles adjacent to each other. To give this building mechanic a purpose, we introduced quests, demanding the player build certain landscape constellations.

What development tools were used to build your game?
====================================================

We used the Unity game engine to develop Dorfromantik. For art asset creation, we used Blender and the Affinity suite. Also, we used many plugins from the Unity Asset store like Odin and DOTween.

What thoughts went into making a game of placing tiles to create villages and landscapes through placing tiles?
===============================================================================================================

All of us enjoy board games, as well as elegantly-designed video games that manage to truly capture the essence of a certain game type. This preference played a big role in shaping Dorfromantik the way it is today.

We chose the setting of a rural village since all of us are very familiar with these kinds of landscapes, growing up in different places in the German and Swiss countryside. We felt like the calming game feel fit the associations and memories we have of those landscapes.

![Image 14](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/blt430d1bddf7da1058/650e783862e65c5e233a2a62/Dorfromantik_203.jpg/?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

How did you design quests around the tile-placing mechanic? 
============================================================

After we settled on the tile-placing mechanic, we collected ideas on how to give the players a challenge and a goal to work towards by placing tiles in a certain way. In our original prototype, we already implemented the basic ideas of counting connected trees, houses, and fields. Later, we refined this idea and placed the quests on the board itself, with them acting like "demands" - the deer wants to live in a forest with at least X trees, the train wants to travel at least X train tracks, etc.

We also had some other criteria the landscape might have to fulfill in mind, but most of them weren't as intuitive and easy-to-communicate as the counting-quests.

What ideas went into creating a sense of progression, and a desire for replay, in the game? 
============================================================================================

With a simple, yet engaging core mechanic in place, we had already covered the first and most important layer of our motivation: the intrinsic motivation. Placing tiles and forming landscapes by itself was already very enjoyable. Since tiles are generated procedurally, the map also ended up looking different with every session.

By adding a high score and an increasing difficulty curve to the game, we also had one way of creating replay value through extrinsic motivation. On top of that, we designed the challenges. They behave like achievements, but are connected to unlockable biomes, tiles, and skins, giving the players additional incentives to try out different play styles. This mechanic is also very extendable, and we have many ideas for new challenges coming up in future updates.

Dorfromantik features many pleasant, tiny animations that make tile placing a joy to do. How did you design these to make tile placement feel good?
===================================================================================================================================================

One of our core philosophies when making games is that the interaction the player does the most has to feel as satisfying as possible. Tiny animations and sound effects are great ways to give the player's actions more impact.

Since we went for an idyllic countryside as a setting, we also wanted the players to enjoy just watching their creation and discovering small details filling it with life.

For all of those additions, we always kept our core ideas in mind and took care that no sound or animation would disrupt the calming atmosphere of Dorfromantik.

![Image 15](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/blt0e98322e2d4f7b46/650e7833a450a127481dcfb0/Dorfromantik_204.jpg/?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

What thoughts went into the visual design of the game? In creating a sense of peace and natural beauty through the look of the game?
====================================================================================================================================

Luca and Zwi created mood boards for our art style, drawing inspiration from landscape paintings and photography. Many artist of the past have done a phenomenal job of capturing the beauty of the countryside and nature in their paintings, often using an idealized way of depicting them. Our intention was the same - to not create a realistic interpretation, but an ideal and harmonic interpretation of the real-world landscapes, with all of their beauty and none of their flaws.

The painted look and haptic aesthetics of Dorfromantik should also emphasize its resemblances to board games.

What thoughts went into designing the game to be relaxing? How did you shape your design to make a game that was challenging, but still calming?
================================================================================================================================================

With Dorfromantik, we wanted to satisfy both types of players: those seeking a challenging puzzle with lots of strategic planning needed, as well as those who enjoy simply building beautiful landscapes. Even within our team, some prefer the one and some the other way of playing.

Because of that, we added several strategic elements to the game, but designed none of them to be too punishing for someone just building for aesthetics. In the future, we will also add a creative mode to make it even easier for players to relax while crafting their ideal little worlds.

Background information

[22](https://www.galaxus.at/en/page/dorfromantik-developer-success-has-opened-a-lot-of-doors-for-us-23775#likes)[6](https://www.galaxus.at/en/page/dorfromantik-developer-success-has-opened-a-lot-of-doors-for-us-23775#comments)

![Image 1: Philipp Rüegg](https://static.digitecgalaxus.ch/im/Files/4/3/6/3/1/4/2/8/TOM_904911.jpg?impolicy=avatar&resizeWidth=40)

Hailing from our very own Switzerland, Sandro Heuberger is co-developer of the indie gaming hit «Dorfromantik». In this interview, he explains how his master’s thesis turned into a full-time project.

The word «Dorfromantik», literally «village romance», has even the best translation apps begging for mercy. The term has any player outside of the German speaking world scratching their head. Nevertheless, the Berlin game studio [Toukana Interactive](https://toukana.com/dorfromantik/) made the decision to keep the original name for its debut work. Even if the majority of the gaming community pronounces it wrong, it’s definitely memorable and fitting to boot. «Dorfromantik» is a PC game that draws on similarities with «The Settlers of Catan» or «Carcassonne». It’s all about building an ever-growing world out of hexagonal cards and letting the high score mount up with perfect card placement. Each little card contains one or more elements such as trees, houses or lakes and ideally should be put on cards with the same elements.

The launch of the early access version a year ago brought the young studio unexpected success. This has created a lot of joy, but also a great deal of work, as ex-Winterthur resident and co-founder Sandro Heuberger tells us.

The interview is also available in audio or video format, starting at 1:28:00.

**«Dorfromantik» was an early access surprise hit. You actually intended to do a classic launch with version 1.0, didn’t you?**  
Sandro Heuberger, co-founder of Toukana: Originally, we wanted to work on the game for a year and then release it. We presented the first content within six months, including a playable demo. There has already been a lot of positive and touching feedback. At the time, we were right in the middle of Covid lockdown. And a lot of people were writing in to tell us that «Dorfromantik» helped them to quieten down and relax. We were really chuffed about this. In fact, it’s what gave us the idea to release the game as early access six months prior to what was planned. During this launch, the store practically blew up in our face – in a positive sense. I still remember opening the Discord server. And you could watch new users joining almost every second. The thing was on fire. It was great, but a lot to take at once.

**At the same time, you cleaned up at the DCP, the German Video Game Awards.**  
That’s right. We won the award for the best debut and also, something that was even more prestigious for us, the prize for the best game design.

**Can you say how many copies of «Dorfromantik» you’ve sold?**  
Put it like this, we were able to repay our funding from the Berlin state in one go. That’s very unusual. Most people manage it, but it takes a long time. We can now stay afloat for two to four years, which is already pretty cool.

[![Image 2: You get bonus points for small quests.](https://static.digitecgalaxus.ch/im/Files/6/3/8/1/5/1/0/6/GIF_Dorfromatik_Gameplay.gif?impolicy=resize&resizeWidth=430)](https://www.galaxus.at/Files/6/3/8/1/5/1/0/6/GIF_Dorfromatik_Gameplay.gif)

You get bonus points for small quests.

**«Dorfromantik» was born out of a degree project. Can you tell me more about that?**  
All four of us completed our bachelor’s in Game Design at HTW Berlin, the University of Applied Sciences. Meanwhile, the master’s course focuses on the entrepreneurial and implementation part of a project. As part of that, we wanted to build a pipeline in order to work on a game for about a year. This included an ideation phase where we developed a new prototype every two or three days within a time frame that was just under three weeks. One of these prototypes was «Dorfromantik».

> For the first few weeks, we did nothing but community management.

**But what took you to Berlin in the first place? I mean, you could have studied game design in Switzerland.**  
I applied to the ZHdK (Zurich University of the Arts). But at that time, you needed to have a preparatory design course under your belt and financially, that just wasn’t an option for me. Once I discovered that, I looked around and, with hindsight, I found the perfect place for me at the HTW in Berlin.

**You sell Dorfromantik through your own channels, without a publisher. Was that never up for discussion?**  
We had the option to work with very well-known and renowned agents. But we made the conscious decision not to take that route because we could already do a lot of the work ourselves in our team of four. For us, it was important to gain as much experience as possible. Our motto is «win or learn». That means we set out to do something and either it works and we’re happy or it goes belly up and we learn from it. It’s like when your mum would tell you a gazillion times not to touch the hot stove. And the lesson only sunk in when the burning feeling sunk into your finger.

[![Image 3: You can also play the game without a time or tile limit.](https://static.digitecgalaxus.ch/im/Files/6/3/8/1/5/1/3/2/Dorfromantik_7.png?impolicy=resize&resizeWidth=430)](https://www.galaxus.at/Files/6/3/8/1/5/1/3/2/Dorfromantik_7.png)

You can also play the game without a time or tile limit.

**After the success of your launch, you must been inundated with partnership requests or even offers to buy you out.**  
Yes – to both those things (laughs). We’ve learnt to get a better handle on it. Initially, we were replying to everything. Now, I ignore repeated requests if I said the first time around that we’d get back to them if we were interested. Success has opened a lot of doors for us.

**Is there still anything where you think you overestimated your abilities?**  
In terms of marketing, we quickly noticed that we needed help. And so, we got someone on board. He’s actually from Switzerland – hey, Marco. Once he got stuck in, we soon felt at ease. Marco has the same ideas as us and was able to give a good impression of us to the outside world.

**I also imagine the topic of community must be very labour-intensive.**  
The community beat a path straight to our door. Don’t get me wrong. It’s nice, but in the first few weeks the four of us did nothing but community management. Of course, it wasn’t a permanent thing. One way or another we also had to finish developing the game. That’s why we have Dom as our dedicated community manager.

**What’s the biggest change the game has seen since early access?**  
We altered the game a lot and added a tonne of content, such as creative mode, which lets you build freely without a high score. That’s especially for players who prefer to build in peace. Our 1.0 launch saw the biggest update yet with the addition of four extra modes, including custom mode. This was our way of thanking the community and letting them create their own modes.

**Now there’s even an undo button. I hear it was incredibly controversial.**  
Requests for an undo button cropped up very early on. Having the option to go a step back – it made sense and was justified. You see, it’s easy to mistype and put down the wrong tile. That can be really annoying when you don’t have 800 tiles spare. But on a technical level, it was difficult to implement because we hadn’t planned this feature from the outset. The undo button was the only thing we never had in beta. And so, we kept it secret until the live release. It was definitely the most popular feature.

**«Dorfromantik» takes its inspiration from board games. Have you ever thought about going in the opposite direction and turning «Dorfromantik» into a board game?**  
We have considered it. Who knows. Maybe there will be something along those lines (laughs).

Dorfromantik: The Board Game Review
===================================

So peaceful
-----------

October 18, 2023

[Justin Bell](https://www.meeplemountain.com/authors/justin-bell/)

5 Min Read

  

[More Board Game Reviews](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/)

Dorfromantik is now both a video game and a board game! Find out what Justin thinks about the 2023 Spiel des Jahres winner in his review.

**Disclosure:** Meeple Mountain received a free copy of this product in exchange for an honest, unbiased review. This review is not intended to be an endorsement.

![Image 6](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/I/51RT0-kWdsL._SL300_.jpg)

[Dorfromantik - The Boardgame](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0BQ3W9GRL?tag=meeplmount-20&linkCode=ogi&th=1&psc=1)

$39.99

[Buy Now](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0BQ3W9GRL?tag=meeplmount-20&linkCode=ogi&th=1&psc=1)

When a game wins a major tabletop award before you review it, you don’t really have much ground to stand on.

The world already agrees that _Dorfromantik: The Board Game_ (2022, [Pegasus Spiele](https://www.meeplemountain.com/publishers/pegasus-spiele/)) is at least a very good game, because it won the prestigious [Spiel des Jahres](https://boardgamegeek.com/awardset/80324/2023-spiel-des-jahres) over the summer.

While there’s always commentary on the games that win this award (in part because there’s always a debate on the shifting sands around the weight of games in this category), time is usually kind to the winners. If you look at the list of winners since [_CATAN_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/articles/games-we-love-catan/) won in 1995, almost every single one is still being celebrated today. This year alone, I’ve been at game nights where we played _Just One, Codenames,_ [_Pictures_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/pictures/), [_Dominion_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/dominion/), [_Hanabi_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/hanabi/), [_Azul_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/azul/), and [_Kingdomino_](https://www.meeplemountain.com/reviews/kingdomino/). Many of these made repeat appearances.

Those are all amazing games. _Dorfromantik: The Board Game_ is no different. That’s because it combines an incredibly simple teach and infinite replayability in a package that can be played solo, multiplayer, campaign-style, and/or as a high-score challenge.

I get it now. _Dorfromantik_ is really good.

![Image 7](https://b1803394.smushcdn.com/1803394/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Dorfromantik-1-1024x768.jpg?lossy=1&strip=1&webp=1)

Spelling Error
--------------

_Dorfromantik_ is a cooperative tile-laying game for 1-6 players, although given the ruleset, I decided to just play this solo.

A series of Task tiles are laid out on the table, face down. These Tasks drive the action of _Dorfromantik_ by asking players to complete, well, tasks—lay five tiles with forest scenery adjacent to at least one edge of another tile featuring forest scenery, for example. To begin the game, three of those Task tiles are placed, adjacent to another Task tile on at least one edge. Then players can either place a Landscape tile, or place another Task tile if there are ever less than three Tasks currently in play.

The landscapes (all of which are shuffled and placed face-down in stacks during setup) come in five flavors: forests, grain, villages, tracks, and streams. Tracks and streams have more rules than the other three terrain types, in that they just can’t run into other terrain types without continuing as tracks or streams. (This becomes obvious when you see the game on the table; who would construct an area where a stream just dead-ends in a village?)

So, turns are simple. Place a tile, try to complete a Task, place more tiles. Each time I sat down to play _Dorfromantik_, I was slowly entranced by the way action plays out. It’s a peaceful puzzle, one that allows for clever play by setting up not only your current Tasks, but your future ones too. In the base game, you have 25 total Task tiles, and five of each of the five terrain types. I regularly found myself flipping tiles and setting up a future where I could knock out a five-tile grain Task, for example, by creating a small section of three or four grain tiles that created a contiguous grain section.

The game ends when you run out of landscape tiles and need to place one. Scores are tallied, with the majority of your score in the base game tied to the total value of the tasks completed. If you wanted to just play a single game, that’s that. You “win” every time you play _Dorfromantik_, but you’re encouraged to play a campaign, and that’s where _Dorfromantik_ really shines: unlockables, and additional ways to give life to extended plays.

![Image 8](https://b1803394.smushcdn.com/1803394/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Dorfromantik-2-768x1024.jpg?lossy=1&strip=1&webp=1)

It’s the Unlocks, Stupid
------------------------

_Dorfromantik_ is a pleasant time at the table, to use a word my colleague [Andrew Lynch](https://www.meeplemountain.com/authors/andrew-lynch/) employs from time to time. I wasn’t wowed by the initial experience, but I admit that it was pleasant to sit at my kitchen table with a glass of wine and listen to classical music in the background.

But if you play _Dorfromantik_ as a campaign game, you add up your scores and log them on a campaign sheet. As you slowly work your way up the cumulative scoring track, you’ll unlock up to five small boxes’ worth of extras. This extra stuff provides a number of different ways to play, challenges to achieve, scoring boosts, and other odds and ends.

In this way, _Dorfromantik_ is like many of the “roguelite” video games I play on my Xbox. You play for 15-20 minutes, die a horrible death (only in those video games…you don’t die in _Dorfromantik_!!), unlock a new skin / power / weapon that grants different playstyles for the next run. And that’s how designers Michael Palm and Lukas Zach get their hooks into you with _Dorfromantik_.

![Image 9](https://b1803394.smushcdn.com/1803394/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Dorfromantik-3-1024x768.jpg?lossy=1&strip=1&webp=1)

During the campaign, you unlock another piece of content every game or two. And you want to get to the end of that campaign sheet, so you think “let me just play one more round tonight” and that turns into another round.

Or four.

_Dorfromantik_ achieves something that not many board games do—create a real hook to play the game over and over again, right away. You can always get a little better each time you play. _Dorfromantik_’s games have usually played out in about 20-25 minutes as a solo game, a little longer if I am deliberate in my approach. At least in the first playthrough, there’s always another small piece of content that required my attention or needed an unlock. Or there’s a challenge that can be completed if I just work a little harder.

You get the idea. I don’t expect to come back to _Dorfromantik_ now that I’ve finished up my review plays, mainly because high-score challenges aren’t my cup of tea. But even as a non-believer, the design here is excellent and the system creates such a great reason to keep coming back.

Well played, _Dorfromantik_. Now I might have to check out the video game to see what I’ve been missing!

##### AUTHOR RATING

*   Great - Would recommend.
